Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette: Seventy‑seven‑year‑old James Kofi, an African American software engineer living with his wife in a quiet suburb, arrived in the United States as a refugee after a brutal civil war in his homeland. For twelve long days he and his family trekked across a desolate border, watching their village burn, hearing distant gunfire and the shrieks of children. One night, a convoy of soldiers seized a bus and, with a sudden burst of gunfire, forced them into the back of a truck that skidded off the road. James remembers the incident as a series of stark images: the flash of fire, the blackness of the night, the shouts of men in uniform, and the sudden, metallic tang of gunpowder. These images persist as snapshots, each one a clear, cold picture he can call up in moments of fear. The day after returning to the United States, James began to feel a jolt whenever he heard a command—whether from a security guard at the office, a colleague ordering him to submit a code review, or a new manager directing the team to meet early. The sudden directive triggers a feeling of detachment, as if he is watching himself from a distance. That same instant, the memory of the convoy appears, and he becomes flooded with the same images, yet he feels utterly numb, as if the scene belongs to someone else. The vivid recall of the violent past forces him to retreat, and he has started to avoid situations where authority figures are present. Because the command activates the traumatic memory, the memory, in turn, intensifies his perception of every directive as a threat, creating a loop that keeps him on edge. To keep his mind occupied, James has adopted a strategy of constant mental distraction. While working, he immerses himself in complex algorithms and debugging tasks, forcing his thoughts to stay within the realm of code. This mental distraction, coupled with a refusal to leave his apartment or engage with people outside the immediate family, keeps him physically and socially isolated. Yet these very coping mechanisms feed back into the traumatic memory. Whenever he experiences a moment of calm, he remembers that it was only because he had avoided a trigger, reinforcing his belief that the world is safer when he remains detached. The memory of the convoy, presented in bright, unfeeling images, continues to haunt him whenever he attempts to distract himself, reminding him of the danger of every command he hears. James’s avoidance has become a self‑fulfilling safeguard. By staying home and shunning office meetings, he reduces the frequency of authority commands, but when the necessity of a work call or an in‑person briefing arrives, the same triggers ignite the traumatic memory once again. The avoidance strategies that he believes protect him instead reinforce his fear of commands, making it more difficult for him to stay engaged in his job. When he does return to the office, his brief encounters with colleagues—particularly when they issue orders—feel like a sudden flashback, and he is forced to withdraw again, perpetuating the cycle of avoidance. For months the pattern has tightened. James’s software engineering tasks suffer as he rushes to finish assignments without reviewing code, fearing that a colleague’s comment might become a command. His wife has noticed that he speaks less about his day, keeps his phone on silent, and refuses to join family dinners. The cumulative isolation has begun to erode the bond that once sustained them. James has reached a point where the constant dread of hearing a directive has begun to dominate his thoughts, and the memory of the convoy remains as vivid as the first day of his escape. He now feels that the only way to break the cycle is to seek help, hoping that learning to process the images and the triggers will let him reclaim the normalcy he once enjoyed in both his personal life and his career.
